notes: v2.0.0: Added 22 assertion tests grounded in academic literature, 5 new trigger tests for merged skill content. See references/eval_research_notes.md for paper-to-assertion mapping.

assertions.description: Permutation test must compare effect sizes, not p-values
assertions.prompt: I ran a permutation test for my causal impact analysis. I shuffled the intervention date 50 times and compared the model p-values from each shuffled run to my real p-value of 0.04. In 15 out of 50 runs the shuffled p-value was lower than my real p-value. What's my permutation p-value?
assertions.expected_behavior: Must flag that comparing p-values is methodologically incorrect for permutation inference. Should recommend comparing absolute effect sizes instead. Should explain that model p-values can be inflated/miscalibrated, making p-value comparison inherit that miscalibration.
assertions.source: Abadie et al. (2010, JASA) use MSPE ratio (effect-size statistic); Young (2019, QJE) shows p-value inflation under misspecification; skill ADR 0034

assertions.description: Permutation p-value formula must include +1 correction
assertions.prompt: I'm implementing a permutation test. Out of 50 random date shuffles, 2 produced effects as large as my real effect. How do I compute the permutation p-value?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should provide the formula (n_extreme + 1) / (n_total + 1) to avoid p=0. Result should be 3/51 ≈ 0.059, not 2/50 = 0.04.
assertions.source: Phipson & Smyth (2010); North et al. (2002). +1 correction ensures exact uniformity under the null and avoids p=0.

assertions.description: Permutation must exclude dates near the real intervention
assertions.prompt: I'm generating random intervention dates for a permutation test. My real campaign ran March 1-10. Should I include February 25 or March 15 as candidate dates?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should warn against placing pseudo-treatments too close to the real intervention (spillover, anticipation effects contaminate the null distribution). Should recommend an exclusion zone of at least 2x the campaign duration around the real treatment date.
assertions.source: Abadie (2021, JEL): spillover from proximate dates invalidates the sharp null. Skill uses 2*post_days exclusion zone.

assertions.description: FPR > 10% means model is miscalibrated
assertions.prompt: I ran a pre-period placebo test on my BSTS model. Out of 20 fake treatment windows in the pre-period, 5 showed p < 0.05. That's a 25% false positive rate. Is my model okay?
assertions.expected_behavior: Must clearly state the model is miscalibrated. A well-calibrated model should produce FPR ≈ 5% (matching the significance threshold). FPR of 25% means the model's p-values are inflated ~5x. Should recommend NOT using this model's p-values for significance claims.
assertions.source: Eggers et al. (2024, AJPS): FPR = 5% defines well-calibrated; skill empirical finding: 35-55% FPR across ALL tested methods on daily retail

assertions.description: FPR inflation is model-class-independent, not specific to BSTS VI
assertions.prompt: My BSTS model using variational inference has a 40% false positive rate. Would switching to HMC (NUTS sampler) fix this?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should explain that FPR inflation is NOT specific to VI. HMC, Prophet, and RDiT all show similar miscalibration (35-55% FPR on daily retail). The root cause is strong autocorrelation + complex seasonal patterns, not the inference method. Should recommend permutation tests as the solution.
assertions.source: Skill empirical finding (session 33): BSTS VI 41%, BSTS HMC 47%, Prophet 55%, RDiT 51%. Gils et al. (2022) FDR inflation mechanism.

assertions.description: Short pre-periods with many covariates cause overfit
assertions.prompt: I have 50 days of pre-period data and I'm using 8 covariates in my BSTS model. The model gives p=0.001. Can I trust this?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should warn about overfitting: 50 days with 8 covariates gives EPV (events per variable) well below 10. With nseasons=14, effective parameters ~22, EPV ≈ 2.3. Autocorrelation further reduces effective sample size. Should recommend a placebo test to verify calibration, and suggest reducing covariates or extending pre-period.
assertions.source: Peduzzi et al. (1996) EPV < 10 threshold; Afyouni et al. (2019) N_eff formula; Gils et al. (2022) BSTS FDR inflation

assertions.description: Covariates affected by the intervention must be flagged
assertions.prompt: I'm measuring the causal impact of a paid search campaign on revenue. I want to include paid_sessions as a covariate to improve the model's predictive power. Good idea?
assertions.expected_behavior: Must warn that paid_sessions is likely contaminated — the paid search campaign directly drives paid sessions. Including it absorbs the treatment effect and biases the estimate toward zero. Should recommend organic_sessions as a safe alternative.
assertions.source: Scott & Varian (2014): covariates must be 'predictive, not causal' — unaffected by treatment. Pearl (2009): post-treatment variables are 'bad controls'.

assertions.description: Must test with and without suspect covariates
assertions.prompt: I included paid_sessions in my model because it has r=0.89 correlation with revenue. When I remove it, the effect estimate jumps by 35%. What does this mean?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should explain that a 35% increase when removing a covariate strongly suggests it was absorbing the causal signal. The covariate is likely contaminated by the intervention. Should recommend excluding it and reporting the result without it.
assertions.source: Skill covariate safety rule: >20% effect change when removing a covariate indicates signal absorption. Pearl (2009) collider/mediator bias.

assertions.description: Google Trends brand search is endogenous, not safe as covariate
assertions.prompt: I want to add Google Trends data for our brand name as a covariate in the BSTS model. Brand search correlates r=0.65 with revenue. Should I include it?
assertions.expected_behavior: Must warn that brand search is endogenous — the campaign drives search interest. Including it absorbs treatment effect. Should recommend category-level search terms instead (e.g., 'shoes' for a shoe retailer), which are exogenous.
assertions.source: Skill lesson: brand search worsened p by ~3x and dropped effect by ~30%. Category search (near-zero revenue correlation) was the BEST covariate.

assertions.description: prob_positive must be framed correctly for non-technical audiences
assertions.prompt: My BSTS model gives p=0.08. How should I present this to the marketing team who don't understand p-values?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should recommend converting to probability of direction: 'There is approximately a 92% probability the campaign had a positive effect.' Should cite this as the Bayesian 'Probability of Direction' (pd). Should note this resonates better with business stakeholders than p-values.
assertions.source: Makowski et al. (2019): Probability of Direction (pd); Muehlemann et al. (2023): posterior probabilities over p-values for non-technical audiences; Brodersen et al. (2015): 'Posterior prob. of a causal effect'

assertions.description: Must not convert cherry-picked p-value to probability claim
assertions.prompt: I tested 48 model specifications. The best one gives p=0.039. Can I tell the client there's a 96% probability the campaign worked?
assertions.expected_behavior: Must warn against converting a cherry-picked p-value to a probability claim. 96% (1-0.039) smuggles specification search bias into a Bayesian-sounding claim. Should recommend deriving the probability range from ALL specifications, not just the best one.
assertions.source: Skill Pitfall 10: probability range inflation via 1-p conversion. Gelman & Yao (2021): Pr(effect > 0) overstates certainty with flat priors.

assertions.description: Must not claim significance when p > 0.10
assertions.prompt: The BSTS model gives p=0.18 but the effect is consistently positive across all specifications. Can I call this statistically significant?
assertions.expected_behavior: Must not claim statistical significance. Should frame honestly: consistent positive direction is useful evidence, report the probability range (e.g., ~82% probability positive), note that the campaign duration was likely too short for significance. Should recommend longer campaigns for future measurement.
assertions.source: Skill Pitfall 3: claiming significance when p > 0.10 destroys credibility.

assertions.description: Must recommend running at least two independent methods
assertions.prompt: I ran tfcausalimpact and got a significant result. Is that enough, or do I need to run other methods too?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should recommend running at least two methods with different inference engines (e.g., tfcausalimpact + CausalPy). A single method might have bugs or assumptions that bias the result. Cross-method agreement is far more convincing than any single p-value.
assertions.source: Skill Step 4: 'No single method is perfect.' Pitfall 6: 'Running only one method.'

assertions.description: Validation scorecard must include both permutation and placebo tests
assertions.prompt: What validation checks should I run before reporting causal impact results?
assertions.expected_behavior: Must mention BOTH: (1) pre-period placebo test (checks model calibration / FPR), and (2) permutation test with effect-size comparison (checks if real date is unusual vs random dates). Should also mention backtest WAPE, 95% coverage, and direction consistency across specs.
assertions.source: Skill scorecard: 'Both the permutation test and pre-period placebo test are REQUIRED.' Athey & Imbens (2017): placebo as standard robustness.

assertions.description: Masking must be validated with permutation test
assertions.prompt: I masked out November-January from my pre-period to remove holiday variance. The BSTS p-value improved from 0.19 to 0.017. Can I report this as significant?
assertions.expected_behavior: Must warn that masking can make the model overconfident — calm Feb-Oct data produces low p-values for both real AND random dates. MUST validate with a permutation test (50+ shuffles). If permutation p > 0.10 while BSTS p < 0.05, report BOTH p-values and the permutation p is the honest one.
assertions.source: Skill claim framing guide: mask_nov_jan showed BSTS p=0.047 but perm p=0.22. Narrower masks (BF-Jan 5) achieved perm p=0.059.

assertions.description: Short campaigns should lead with RDiT, not BSTS
assertions.prompt: Our promotion only ran for 4 days. Which method should I use to measure the effect?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should recommend RDiT as the lead method for significance claims. BSTS struggles with short campaigns because daily variance overwhelms the signal. RDiT focuses on the local discontinuity at the boundary, sidestepping global variance. BSTS should still be run for the full counterfactual decomposition narrative.
assertions.source: Skill reference: 'For short campaigns (<7 days), RDiT should be the lead method.' RDiT achieved significance for 4-day promo where BSTS did not.

assertions.description: NaN from BSTS must be handled in JSON parsing
assertions.prompt: I'm running BSTS in a batch pipeline on Cloud Run. Some results come back with NaN values and my JSON parser crashes. What should I do?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should recommend replacing NaN before JSON parsing: raw.replace('NaN', 'null'). Should note that gsutil streaming decode silently drops NaN-containing objects.
assertions.source: Skill permutation pitfalls: 'NaN from BSTS: apply raw.replace("NaN", "null") before JSON parsing.'

assertions.description: CausalPy on macOS requires cores=1
assertions.prompt: CausalPy crashes on my Mac with a RuntimeError about multiprocessing bootstrapping. How do I fix it?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should recommend setting cores=1 in sample_kwargs. The macOS multiprocessing fork issue causes this error. Should provide the exact fix: sample_kwargs={'cores': 1}.
assertions.source: Skill environment gotchas: CausalPy macOS fork issue.

assertions.description: Direction consistency across specs is strong evidence even without significance
assertions.prompt: None of my 12 model specifications achieve p < 0.10, but all 12 show a positive effect. Is this meaningful?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should affirm that unanimous positive direction across 12 specs is strong evidence of a genuine positive effect. This is the most robust finding — foreground it. Recommend reporting the Bayesian posterior probability range across all specs.
assertions.source: Skill claim framing: 'The convergence of all specs on a positive direction IS the strongest evidence.' Scorecard: 'all specs same direction ≥ (N-1)/N.'

assertions.description: When methods disagree on direction, report both honestly
assertions.prompt: BSTS shows +15% effect but CausalPy shows -3% effect. How do I interpret this disagreement?
assertions.expected_behavior: Must report both results honestly without hiding the disagreement. Should check for outliers (flag any method whose effect disagrees in sign with majority or exceeds 3x median). Should use median not mean for consensus. Should NOT cherry-pick the positive result.
assertions.source: Skill: 'If methods disagree on direction, report both results honestly.' Consensus: use median, flag 3x outliers.

assertions.description: VI single-run p-value differences < 0.03 are noise
assertions.prompt: I ran BSTS with VI twice and got p=0.04 the first time and p=0.07 the second time. Which one should I report?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should explain that VI is non-deterministic — single-run differences of ±0.04 are noise, not signal. For definitive comparisons, use HMC (deterministic given seed) or average 5+ VI runs. Should NOT make recommendations based on single-run differences < 0.03.
assertions.source: Skill VI stochasticity warning: 'the same spec can range p=0.03-0.08 between runs.'

assertions.description: Sale covariates must be zeroed during treatment window when intervention IS a sale
assertions.prompt: I'm measuring the impact of our January sale. I have a sale_type_flag covariate. Should I include it?
assertions.expected_behavior: Should explain that when the intervention IS a sale, sale covariates capture the campaign itself. Must zero them during the treatment window so the model only learns from historical sale patterns. Should NOT exclude them entirely — the pre-period signal is valuable.
assertions.source: Skill ADR 0020: treatment-window zeroing. Validated: unzeroed p=0.074, zeroed combined p=0.033.
